title: CIMA BA1 - Fundamentals of Business Economics
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the CIMA BA1 syllabus (business economics). Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: A country reports that nominal gross domestic product grew by 5 percent over the year while the general price level also rose by 5 percent. Which conclusion about real output is most accurate?
options: Real output was broadly unchanged because the growth was entirely price inflation
Real output grew by 10 percent because both figures must be added together
Real output fell by 5 percent because prices rose during the year
Real output cannot be inferred from nominal GDP under any circumstances
items.explanation: Real growth is nominal growth net of inflation, so 5 percent minus 5 percent leaves real output essentially flat. Adding the two figures double counts the effect, and real output can be estimated by deflating nominal GDP by a price index.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: A government increases its spending sharply while the central bank holds interest rates unchanged, and firms cannot raise output quickly. Which type of inflation is most likely to result?
options: Cost-push inflation caused by rising import prices
Demand-pull inflation caused by excess aggregate demand
Structural inflation caused by a fall in the labour force
Imported inflation caused by a weaker exchange rate
items.explanation: Extra government spending raises aggregate demand faster than output can respond, pulling prices upward. Cost-push and imported inflation stem from rising input or import costs rather than from demand pressure.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: A sharp rise in global oil prices raises transport and energy costs across an economy. Which type of inflation does this best illustrate?
options: Deflation from falling aggregate demand
Demand-pull inflation from higher consumer incomes
Cost-push inflation from higher input prices
Hyperinflation from excessive money printing
items.explanation: Higher oil prices raise firms' production and distribution costs, which they pass on as higher prices, so this is cost-push inflation. Demand-pull inflation arises from spending rather than from costs.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: Which statement best describes the consumer prices index when it is used as a measure of inflation?
options: It records the total value of goods exported during the year
It measures the unemployment rate among working-age adults
It shows the interest rate set by the central bank
It tracks the prices of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by a typical household
items.explanation: A consumer prices index follows a representative basket of household purchases and monitors how its cost changes over time. Export values, unemployment and central bank rates are measured by entirely different statistics.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: A skilled worker leaves one job and spends three weeks searching before starting a better-paid role. Which category of unemployment does this represent?
options: Frictional unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
items.explanation: Short spells while moving between jobs are frictional unemployment and are normal in a healthy labour market. Structural unemployment reflects a mismatch of skills, while cyclical unemployment follows a downturn in demand.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: An economy's textile industry closes permanently because cheaper imports dominate the market, and former workers lack the skills demanded elsewhere. Which type of unemployment is this?
options: Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Voluntary unemployment
items.explanation: A lasting change in the pattern of industry combined with a skills mismatch produces structural unemployment. Frictional unemployment is short-lived job search, and cyclical unemployment tracks the business cycle.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: During a deep recession, falling consumer demand leads many firms to make workers redundant across several industries. Which type of unemployment is most evident?
options: Structural unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
items.explanation: Redundancies driven by a general fall in demand are cyclical unemployment because they rise and fall with the business cycle. Structural unemployment would persist even after demand recovers, because it reflects a mismatch of skills.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: According to the short-run Phillips curve, what relationship is generally observed between inflation and unemployment?
options: Higher inflation always raises unemployment at the same time
The inflation rate and the unemployment rate are always identical
There is no recognised relationship between the two at all
Higher inflation tends to be associated with lower unemployment
items.explanation: The short-run Phillips curve shows a trade-off in which lower unemployment is typically accompanied by higher inflation. The two rates are not equal, and policy attempts to exploit the trade-off only work temporarily.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: A government facing high unemployment decides to cut taxes and increase public spending on infrastructure. Which policy stance does this represent?
options: Expansionary fiscal policy
Contractionary fiscal policy
Expansionary monetary policy
Contractionary monetary policy
items.explanation: Cutting taxes and raising spending are fiscal tools used to stimulate demand, so this is expansionary fiscal policy. Monetary policy would instead involve interest rates or money supply, and contractionary policy would withdraw demand.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: When a government's total spending exceeds its tax revenue in a financial year, the resulting shortfall is best described as which of the following?
options: A trade surplus
A budget deficit
A balance of payments surplus
A budget surplus
items.explanation: Spending above tax revenue gives a budget deficit, which is normally financed by borrowing. A surplus is the opposite outcome, and a trade balance concerns exports and imports rather than the public finances.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: A central bank raises its policy interest rate to reduce inflationary pressure. Through which main channel is this expected to work?
options: By raising the value of exports directly
By lowering the cost of credit for households
By making borrowing more expensive and reducing aggregate demand
By increasing government spending automatically
items.explanation: Higher rates raise the cost of borrowing, discourage spending and investment, and so dampen aggregate demand and inflation. Government spending is a fiscal matter, and cheaper credit would be the result of cutting rates.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: When a central bank buys government bonds from financial institutions in order to inject money into the economy, this policy is known as what?
options: Fiscal consolidation
Open outcry trading
Prudential regulation
Quantitative easing
items.explanation: Quantitative easing is the purchase of assets by a central bank to expand the money supply when interest rates are already very low. Fiscal consolidation concerns cutting government borrowing, and prudential regulation supervises bank safety.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: Which statement best explains the link between rapid growth in the money supply and inflation in the long run?
options: More money in circulation with limited output growth tends to push the general price level up
More money in circulation always reduces the general price level
The money supply has no influence on prices at all
Inflation is caused only by changes in the weather
items.explanation: If money grows much faster than the volume of goods and services, the extra purchasing power tends to bid prices upward. Money growth does not automatically lower prices, and inflation is not driven by weather.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: A country's earnings from exports of goods and services plus net income and transfers are less than its spending on imports and similar outflows. Which term describes this situation?
options: A capital account deficit
A current account deficit
A current account surplus
A budget surplus
items.explanation: When inflows on the current account fall short of outflows, the country runs a current account deficit. A surplus is the reverse position, and the budget position relates to government revenue and spending rather than trade.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: A country's currency depreciates against its main trading partners while its exports remain price sensitive. What is the most likely effect on its export competitiveness?
options: There is no effect on the price of exports abroad
Exports stop completely following the depreciation
Exports become cheaper for foreign buyers and more competitive
Exports become more expensive for foreign buyers
items.explanation: A depreciation lowers the foreign-currency price of exports, which should raise demand when buyers are price sensitive. The opposite effect would follow an appreciation, and trade does not cease simply because a currency weakens.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: Two countries can both produce cloth and wine, but each sacrifices less of the other good when specialising in one product. What principle explains why specialisation and trade can benefit both countries?
options: Absolute disadvantage
Protectionism
Diminishing returns
Comparative advantage
items.explanation: Comparative advantage explains gains from trade when each country specialises where its opportunity cost is lowest. Protectionism restricts trade, and diminishing returns concerns additional units of a variable input.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: A government imposes a tax on imported steel in order to protect domestic producers. What is this trade measure called?
options: A tariff
A quota
An embargo
A subsidy
items.explanation: A tariff is a tax on imports that raises their price and shelters domestic firms. A quota limits quantity rather than price, a subsidy supports domestic output, and an embargo bans trade altogether.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: A group of countries agrees to remove tariffs among its members while keeping a common external tariff against non-members. Which form of economic integration is this?
options: A free trade area
A customs union
A common market
An economic union
items.explanation: A customs union combines free trade internally with a common external tariff. A free trade area removes internal tariffs but lets members set their own external tariffs, while a common market also frees the movement of labour and capital.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: An economy moves from a peak into a period of falling output and rising unemployment before recovering. What is this recurring pattern called?
options: The multiplier effect
The law of one price
The business or trade cycle
The Phillips curve
items.explanation: The business cycle describes the recurring sequence of expansion, peak, contraction and recovery in economic activity. The Phillips curve links inflation and unemployment, and the multiplier magnifies an initial change in spending.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: Which factor would most directly increase an economy's long-run productive capacity?
options: A rise in the general price level
An increase in the money supply on its own
An increase in the number of public holidays
An increase in investment in capital goods and workforce skills
items.explanation: Long-run capacity grows through more or better capital, labour and technology, so investment in capital goods and skills is the key driver. Higher prices or extra money do not create new productive resources.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Macroeconomic Context of Business

items.stem: A rise in consumers' disposable incomes leads households to buy more of a normal good at every price. How is this best described on a demand diagram?
options: A rightward shift of the demand curve
A leftward shift of the demand curve
A movement along the supply curve
A movement along the demand curve
items.explanation: A change in a determinant other than price, such as income, shifts the whole demand curve, and greater demand at every price shifts it right. A movement along the curve would be caused by a change in the good's own price.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: The price of coffee falls and, with no other change, consumers buy more of it. How is this best represented?
options: A shift of the supply curve
A movement along the demand curve
A shift of the demand curve to the right
A shift of the demand curve to the left
items.explanation: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along its demand curve rather than a shift. Shifts of demand are caused only by changes in other determinants such as income, tastes or the prices of related goods.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: A new technology lowers the cost of producing solar panels at every output level. How is this best shown on a supply diagram?
options: A movement up along the supply curve
A leftward shift of the supply curve
A rightward shift of the supply curve
A leftward shift of the demand curve
items.explanation: Lower production costs make firms willing to supply more at every price, so the supply curve shifts right. A movement along the curve would reflect a change in price, and a leftward supply shift would indicate higher costs.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: In a competitive market, the price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied is known as what?
options: The maximum price
The administered price
The transfer price
The equilibrium price
items.explanation: The equilibrium price clears the market because the quantities buyers want and sellers offer are equal. A maximum price is a regulatory ceiling, and a transfer price is used for internal transactions within a firm.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: The price of a good rises from 10 to 12 and, as a result, the quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80 units. Using the simple percentage change method, what is the price elasticity of demand expressed as a positive number?
items.explanation: Quantity demanded falls by 20 percent while price rises by 20 percent, so elasticity equals 1.0 and demand is unit elastic. A value of 2.0 would require quantity to change twice as much as price in percentage terms.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: Which good is most likely to have an inelastic demand because buyers have few substitutes and it takes only a small share of household income?
options: A luxury sports car
Table salt
An overseas holiday
A particular brand of bottled water
items.explanation: Salt has few substitutes, is a small part of the budget and is a necessity, so its demand is inelastic. Luxury and branded goods have closer substitutes and larger budget shares, making their demand more elastic.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: A firm faces inelastic demand for its product and raises its price. What is the most likely effect on its total revenue?
options: Total revenue will remain exactly the same
Total revenue will fall to zero
Total revenue will rise because the fall in quantity is proportionally smaller
Total revenue will fall because quantity demanded collapses
items.explanation: With inelastic demand the percentage fall in quantity is smaller than the percentage rise in price, so revenue increases. Revenue falls with a price rise only when demand is elastic, and it cannot drop to zero from a modest price change.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: A good has an income elasticity of demand of minus 0.8. What does this indicate about the good?
options: It is a luxury good
It has perfectly elastic demand
It is a normal good
It is an inferior good
items.explanation: A negative income elasticity means demand falls as income rises, which defines an inferior good. Normal and luxury goods have positive income elasticities, and perfect elasticity would give an infinite value.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: The cross elasticity of demand between two goods is positive. What does this suggest about their relationship?
options: They are substitutes
They are unrelated
They are both inferior goods
They are complements
items.explanation: A positive cross elasticity means a rise in the price of one good increases demand for the other, which is the pattern for substitutes. Complements have a negative cross elasticity because they are used together.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: Which situation best describes a price elasticity of supply greater than one?
options: Supply is perfectly inelastic in the short run
Quantity supplied changes proportionally more than price, so supply is elastic
Quantity supplied does not change when price changes
Quantity supplied falls whenever the price rises
items.explanation: Elastic supply means producers respond strongly to price, so quantity changes proportionally more than price. A value of zero is perfectly inelastic, and supply curves normally slope upward rather than falling as price rises.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: A manufacturer pays 20,000 in annual factory rent regardless of output and 15 in materials for each unit produced. How are these costs best classified?
options: Both rent and materials are fixed costs
Both rent and materials are variable costs
Rent is a fixed cost and materials are a variable cost
Rent is a variable cost and materials are a fixed cost
items.explanation: Rent does not change with output, so it is fixed, while materials rise with each unit produced and are variable. Swapping the classifications ignores how each cost behaves as output changes.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: What does the concept of marginal cost measure?
options: The cost that does not vary with the level of output
The revenue obtained from selling one more unit
Total cost divided by the number of units produced
The additional cost of producing one more unit of output
items.explanation: Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one additional unit of output. Total cost divided by output is average cost, and the revenue from an extra unit is marginal revenue rather than cost.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: A firm produces 500 units at a total cost of 25,000. What is its average cost per unit?
items.explanation: Average cost equals total cost divided by output, so 25,000 divided by 500 equals 50 per unit. The other figures result from dividing in the wrong direction or misplacing the decimal point.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: As a firm's output rises, its long-run average cost falls because it can spread fixed costs and use more efficient machinery. This is an example of what?
options: Marginal cost pricing
Economies of scale
Diseconomies of scale
Diminishing returns
items.explanation: A fall in long-run average cost as output grows reflects economies of scale. Diseconomies of scale would raise average cost, and diminishing returns relate to a variable input added to a fixed factor in the short run.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: A firm grows so large that coordination and communication problems raise its long-run average cost. What does this illustrate?
options: Price discrimination
Economies of scale
Diseconomies of scale
Constant returns to scale
items.explanation: When expansion pushes long-run average cost upward, the firm suffers diseconomies of scale, often from management and coordination difficulties. Economies of scale would lower average cost as output rises.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: Adding more workers to a fixed amount of machinery eventually causes each extra worker to add less output than the one before. Which principle does this describe?
options: Economies of scale
The law of one price
Comparative advantage
The law of diminishing marginal returns
items.explanation: Diminishing marginal returns occur in the short run when extra units of a variable input are added to a fixed factor, so each additional worker adds less output. Economies of scale concern the long run when all factors can change.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: Which feature is characteristic of a perfectly competitive market?
options: Many small firms sell an identical product and are price takers
Products are heavily differentiated through branding
Entry by new firms is completely blocked
A single seller sets the market price
items.explanation: Perfect competition features many firms, a homogeneous product, free entry and no individual price-setting power. A single seller describes monopoly, and product differentiation or blocked entry point to other structures.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: A single firm supplies the entire market for a product that has no close substitutes and is protected by high barriers to entry. What market structure is this?
options: Oligopoly
Monopoly
Perfect competition
Monopolistic competition
items.explanation: One seller, no close substitutes and high entry barriers define a monopoly. Oligopoly involves a few large firms, and monopolistic competition involves many firms selling differentiated products with free entry.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: Many firms sell similar but differentiated products, each with some pricing power, and new firms can enter freely in the long run. Which market structure best fits?
options: Oligopoly
Perfect competition
Monopolistic competition
Monopoly
items.explanation: Product differentiation with many sellers and free entry is the hallmark of monopolistic competition. Perfect competition has identical products, while monopoly and oligopoly involve one or few sellers respectively.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: A market is dominated by a small number of large firms whose decisions about price and output are interdependent. What is this market structure called?
options: Monopsony
Perfect competition
Monopoly
Oligopoly
items.explanation: A few interdependent sellers characterise oligopoly, where each firm must consider rivals' reactions. Monopoly has a single seller, and monopsony refers to a single buyer rather than a dominant seller.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: In the kinked demand curve model of oligopoly, why are prices often described as sticky?
options: Rivals match price cuts but not price rises, so firms lose out whichever way they move
The government fixes all prices by law
Firms are unable to calculate their own costs
There is only one buyer in the whole market
items.explanation: When rivals follow a price cut but ignore a price rise, a firm gains little from cutting and loses sales from raising, so prices stay stable. This is a behavioural result, not a legal price control or a single-buyer situation.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: An airline charges business travellers a higher fare than leisure travellers for seats on the same flight. What is this practice called?
options: Cross-subsidisation
Price discrimination
Predatory pricing
Price skimming
items.explanation: Charging different prices to different groups for the same service, based on their willingness to pay, is price discrimination. Predatory pricing aims to drive out rivals, and price skimming sets a high initial price for a new product.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: Using the marginal approach, at which point does a firm maximise its profit?
options: Where total revenue reaches its maximum
Where marginal cost falls to zero
Where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
Where average cost is at its highest
items.explanation: Profit is maximised where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, because producing beyond that point adds more to cost than to revenue. Maximum revenue ignores costs, and highest average cost is where unit costs are worst.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: What does consumer surplus measure in a market?
options: The total revenue received by producers
The tax paid by consumers on a good
The profit earned by a monopolist
The difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay
items.explanation: Consumer surplus is the benefit buyers enjoy when they pay less than their maximum willingness to pay. Producer revenue and monopoly profit accrue to sellers, while tax is a transfer to government.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: A factory's production creates pollution that harms local residents, but the harm is not reflected in the price of its product. What does this illustrate?
options: Market failure arising from a negative externality
A perfectly competitive market outcome
A gain in consumer surplus
An increase in producer surplus
items.explanation: An uncharged cost imposed on third parties is a negative externality, and because the price ignores it the market fails to allocate resources efficiently. Perfect competition and surplus measures assume costs and benefits are fully reflected in prices.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Microeconomic and Market Forces

items.stem: What is the main economic function of a financial system?
options: To guarantee that every investment is profitable
To channel funds from savers to borrowers and to facilitate payments
To set the level of government taxation
To fix the price of all goods and services
items.explanation: A financial system moves funds from surplus units to deficit units and provides payment and risk-transfer services. Taxation is a government fiscal function, and no system can guarantee investment profits.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: Which of the following is normally traded in the money market?
options: Ordinary shares listed on a stock exchange
Residential mortgages held for many years
Short-term debt instruments with maturities of up to about one year
Long-term government bonds with thirty-year maturities
items.explanation: The money market deals in short-term, highly liquid instruments such as treasury bills and commercial paper. Long-dated bonds and shares belong to the capital market, and mortgages are long-term loans.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: Which market is primarily concerned with long-term securities such as shares and long-dated bonds?
options: The foreign exchange market
The interbank payment system
The money market
The capital market
items.explanation: The capital market raises and trades long-term finance, including equities and bonds. The money market handles short-term funds, while the foreign exchange market trades currencies.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: How do commercial banks mainly earn profit when acting as financial intermediaries?
options: By paying depositors a lower rate than they charge borrowers
By printing new currency on behalf of the central bank
By setting the official interest rate for the economy
By collecting taxes on behalf of the government
items.explanation: Banks borrow from depositors at low rates and lend at higher rates, earning the interest margin. Currency issuance and official interest rates are central bank functions, and tax collection is a government role.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: Which function is normally carried out by a country's central bank?
options: Setting the rates of income tax
Setting monetary policy and acting as lender of last resort
Selling life insurance policies to households
Auditing the accounts of every private company
items.explanation: Central banks set monetary policy, issue currency and provide emergency liquidity to the banking system. Insurance is sold by commercial insurers, auditing is performed by audit firms, and taxation is set by government.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between existing bond prices and market interest rates?
options: Bond prices are completely unaffected by interest rates
Bond prices change only when the issuer is liquidated
When market interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds tend to fall
When market interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds also rise
items.explanation: A rise in market rates makes a bond's fixed coupon less attractive, so its price falls until the yield matches the market. The relationship is inverse, so prices are not insensitive to interest rates.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: Which statement best describes a bond?
options: An ownership stake in a company
A short-term deposit placed with a bank
A government subsidy paid to a private firm
A loan to an issuer that pays interest and repays principal at maturity
items.explanation: A bond is a debt instrument that pays the holder interest and returns principal at maturity. An ownership stake is an equity share, and deposits and subsidies are different financial arrangements.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: Which statement best describes an ordinary share?
options: It represents part-ownership of a company and carries a residual claim on profits
It is a fixed-interest loan repayable at a set date
It guarantees a fixed dividend to the holder each year
It is issued only by central banks
items.explanation: Ordinary shares are equity, so holders own part of the company and receive dividends only after other claims are met. Fixed interest and repayment at a set date are features of debt, not equity.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: What is the main purpose of regulating financial institutions and markets?
options: To maximise the profits of commercial banks
To maintain stability, protect consumers and reduce systemic risk
To guarantee above-market returns for investors
To prevent all forms of financial innovation
items.explanation: Regulation aims to keep the financial system safe and fair by protecting customers and containing risks that could spread through the system. It does not promise returns, block all innovation or prioritise bank profits.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: Requiring banks to hold a minimum amount of capital relative to their risk-weighted assets is an example of what kind of regulation?
options: Monetary easing
Fiscal policy
Prudential regulation
Conduct regulation
items.explanation: Prudential regulation focuses on the safety and soundness of financial firms, including capital adequacy. Conduct regulation governs how firms treat customers, while easing and fiscal policy are macroeconomic tools.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: The international framework that sets minimum capital standards for banks is associated with which body?
options: The World Trade Organization
The International Labour Organization
The United Nations Security Council
The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision
items.explanation: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision publishes the Basel capital standards adopted by regulators worldwide. The other bodies deal with trade, labour and international security rather than bank capital rules.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: What is the main purpose of a deposit insurance scheme?
options: To protect small depositors if a bank fails and to reduce the risk of bank runs
To increase the interest rate paid on savings accounts
To fund government spending during a recession
To set tariffs on imported goods
items.explanation: Deposit insurance repays savers up to a limit if their bank fails, which reassures them and makes sudden withdrawals less likely. It is not a tool for setting interest rates, funding deficits or controlling trade.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: Which of the following would normally be included in a broad measure of the money supply?
options: The total value of a country's exports
Currency in circulation plus bank deposits
Only the notes and coins held by the central bank
Company shares and government bonds
items.explanation: Broad money includes currency in circulation together with deposits held at banks and other institutions. Shares and bonds are financial assets rather than money, and export values measure trade.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: Where is the price of one currency expressed in terms of another normally determined?
options: In the primary market for corporate bonds
In the labour market for skilled workers
In the foreign exchange market
In the money market for treasury bills
items.explanation: Exchange rates are set in the foreign exchange market, where currencies are bought and sold continuously. The money and bond markets price short-term and long-term debt, and the labour market prices work.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation

items.stem: What is the main role of a stock exchange?
options: To lend money directly to households for house purchases
To set the level of interest rates in the economy
To issue currency on behalf of the government
To provide a regulated marketplace where securities can be bought and sold
items.explanation: A stock exchange is an organised secondary market that lets investors trade listed securities under a common rulebook. Lending to households, setting interest rates and issuing currency are functions of banks and the central bank.
items.reference: CIMA BA1 Syllabus - Financial Markets, Institutions and Regulation
